title: What Dissolves? Solute, Solvent, and Safety
summary: Learners make and describe solutions, measure solute and solvent, test how heat affects dissolving, use litmus to classify acids and bases, and practice safe use of lab equipment.

competencies.text: Identify the role of the solute and solvent in a solution.
Express quantitatively the amount of solute present in a given volume of solvent.
Demonstrate how different factors affect the solubility of a solute in a given solvent, such as heat;
Identify solutions, which can be found at home and in school and that react with a litmus indicator, as acids, bases, and salts.
Demonstrate proper use and handling of science equipment.

timing.basis: Science is taught five times a week, 45 minutes a session, in Grades 3–10: DepEd Order No. 010, s. 2024 (Tables 3, 5 and 6) and DepEd Order No. 012, s. 2024 (§2.a, which also allows uniform 50, 55 or 60-minute periods). Applied to the SY 2026–2027 three-term calendar.

guide.bigIdea: A solution forms when a solute spreads evenly into a solvent. How much solute can dissolve, how fast it dissolves, and how the solution responds to litmus depend on the identity of the substances and the conditions.
guide.whyItMatters: Solutions are everywhere in Philippine life—salt water for cooking and preserving, sugar in drinks, vinegar and calamansi as acids, baking soda as a base. Understanding solute and solvent helps learners prepare safe, effective solutions at home and make sense of mixtures in the environment.

background.heading: What a solution is at the particle level
paragraphs: A solution is a homogeneous mixture, meaning it looks the same throughout. At the particle level, the particles of the substance being dissolved separate and spread evenly among the particles of the substance doing the dissolving. In sugar water, individual sugar molecules become surrounded by water molecules. The mixture appears clear and uniform because the particles are too small to see, and they do not settle out.

This is different from a suspension like sand in water, where the sand particles are large enough to settle to the bottom. A solution is stable—once formed, the solute remains distributed throughout the solvent as long as conditions do not change.

background.heading: Solute and solvent roles
paragraphs: The solute is the substance that dissolves. The solvent is the substance that does the dissolving. In a salt and water mixture, salt is the solute and water is the solvent. Water is often called the universal solvent because more substances dissolve in water than in any other common liquid. This happens because water molecules are polar, meaning they have a slightly positive side and a slightly negative side, which helps them attract and surround many ionic and polar solute particles.

Many solutions are liquid, but not all. Air is a gas solution in which nitrogen is the solvent and oxygen, carbon dioxide, and other gases are solutes. Brass and sterling silver are solid solutions of metals. In every case, the solute is the smaller amount being dispersed, and the solvent is the larger amount doing the dispersing.

background.heading: How much can dissolve: concentration and solubility
paragraphs: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a specific temperature. Concentration, on the other hand, is the actual amount of solute in a certain amount of solution. Concentration can be expressed in many ways; for this week learners use percent mass per volume, which means grams of solute per 100 mL of solution.

For example, at room temperature, 100 mL of water can dissolve about 36 grams of table salt. If only 5 grams of salt are dissolved in 100 mL of water, the solution is unsaturated and the concentration is about 5% mass/volume. If learners keep adding salt until no more dissolves and some settles at the bottom, the solution is saturated.

Teachers should be aware that most concentration calculations assume the final solution volume, not just the solvent volume. For dilute aqueous solutions, the difference is small, but for accurate work, percent concentration compares the amount of solute to the total solution volume, not the solvent volume alone. Textbooks sometimes simplify this and say 'per 100 mL of water', which is acceptable for Grade 7 as long as the lesson does not require precise quantitative work.

background.heading: Temperature and the rate of dissolving
paragraphs: Heating a solvent usually makes solid solutes dissolve faster because the solvent particles move faster and collide with solute particles more often. For many solids, heating also increases the maximum amount that can dissolve—the solubility. However, stirring and crushing the solute only speed up the process; they do not change the solubility limit.

For gases dissolved in liquids, the opposite is true: warmer water holds less dissolved gas than cold water. This is why warm soft drinks lose their fizz quickly. This week focuses on heat as a factor affecting solubility of solid solutes, so teachers may mention the gas exception but should not expect learners to calculate gas solubility.

background.heading: Acids, bases, salts, and litmus
paragraphs: Acids are substances that release hydrogen ions when dissolved in water. Bases release hydroxide ions or accept hydrogen ions. Salts are ionic compounds produced when an acid reacts with a base in a neutralization reaction. Litmus is an indicator—a substance that changes color in the presence of an acid or a base. Blue litmus paper turns red in an acid. Red litmus paper turns blue in a base. A neutral solution, like table salt solution, generally does not change the color of either paper.

Common household acids include vinegar (acetic acid) and calamansi juice (citric acid). Baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) dissolved in water is a base. Table salt (sodium chloride) dissolved in water is a neutral salt. Teachers should emphasize that learners must never taste a solution to identify it; litmus paper is the safe, observable test.

misconceptions.belief: The solute disappears when it dissolves.
misconceptions.whyLearnersThinkIt: They cannot see the salt or sugar after stirring.
misconceptions.correctIdea: The solute is still present; its particles are spread evenly among the solvent particles.
misconceptions.howToAddress: Weigh the cup with water AND the salt separately, then weigh the cup after the salt has dissolved. The final mass equals cup + water + salt. Nothing was lost, even though the salt can no longer be seen.

misconceptions.belief: Stirring increases the amount of solute that can dissolve.
misconceptions.whyLearnersThinkIt: When they stir, more solute seems to dissolve faster.
misconceptions.correctIdea: Stirring only speeds up dissolving. It does not change solubility. The maximum amount depends on the solute, solvent, and temperature.
misconceptions.howToAddress: Have learners add sugar to two cups, one stirred and one left still. After enough time, both reach the same maximum amount dissolved.

misconceptions.belief: All acids are dangerous and all bases are safe.
misconceptions.whyLearnersThinkIt: The word 'acid' sounds harmful, while common bases like baking soda seem harmless.
misconceptions.correctIdea: Both strong acids and strong bases can be corrosive. Weak acids and weak bases are common in food and cleaning products.
misconceptions.howToAddress: Show vinegar (weak acid) and baking soda (weak base). Explain that concentrated drain cleaner is a dangerous base, so both types must be handled with care.

misconceptions.belief: Red litmus paper turns blue in an acid.
misconceptions.whyLearnersThinkIt: They mix up which color changes in which type of solution.
misconceptions.correctIdea: Blue litmus turns red in an acid; red litmus turns blue in a base.
misconceptions.howToAddress: Use a color chart and have learners test a known acid and a known base. Repeat the rule aloud each time.

studentQuestions.question: If I keep adding salt to water, will it all dissolve?
studentQuestions.answer: No. Water can hold only a certain amount of salt at a given temperature. That point is called saturation. Extra salt will settle at the bottom.

studentQuestions.question: Why does sugar dissolve faster in warm water than cold water?
studentQuestions.answer: Warm water particles move faster and bump into sugar particles more often. This pulls the sugar into solution more quickly.

studentQuestions.question: Does stirring make more solute dissolve?
studentQuestions.answer: Stirring makes solute dissolve faster because it brings fresh solvent into contact with the solute. But stirring does not change the maximum amount that can dissolve at that temperature.

studentQuestions.question: Why do we use litmus paper instead of tasting a solution to know if it is an acid or a base?
studentQuestions.answer: Tasting unknown chemicals is never safe. Litmus paper is a safe, quick way to test whether a solution is acidic or basic without putting it in your mouth.

studentQuestions.question: Is seawater a solution? What is the solute and what is the solvent?
studentQuestions.answer: Yes, seawater is a solution. Water is the solvent, and the dissolved salts—mostly sodium chloride—are the solutes.

localExamples.example: Salt making in coastal areas: people evaporate seawater to collect salt.
localExamples.connection: Seawater is a solution. Evaporation removes the solvent (water), leaving behind the solute (salt).

localExamples.example: Calamansi juice used in Filipino cooking is sour because of citric acid.
localExamples.connection: Calamansi juice is an acid. Blue litmus paper turns red in it.

localExamples.example: Warm water for washing dishes dissolves sugar or coffee residue faster than cold water.
localExamples.connection: Heat increases the rate at which a solid solute dissolves.

localExamples.example: Baking soda dissolved in water is used for cleaning and in baking.
localExamples.connection: Baking soda solution is a base. Red litmus paper turns blue in it.

preparation: Before Day 1: Pre-measure salt and sugar into small labeled cups. Fill a thermos with warm (not boiling) water for Day 3. Test litmus paper with vinegar and baking soda solution to ensure it works.
Before Day 2: Set up measuring stations with graduated cylinders or measuring cups. Have room-temperature water ready.
Before Day 3: Prepare warm water and cold tap water. Have identical cups and spoons ready.
Before Day 4: Prepare solutions to test: vinegar, calamansi juice, baking soda solution, and salt solution. Cut litmus strips into small pieces if needed.

Before Day 5: Print or write assessment items. Prepare materials for the performance task planning session, such as a shallow dish and a small amount of salt water if learners will set up evaporation.
safety: Do not taste or drink any test solutions. Wash hands with soap and water after handling chemicals and litmus paper.
Use warm water, not boiling water, to avoid burns. The teacher should check the temperature before learners handle it.
Handle glass graduated cylinders with care. Place them on a flat surface when reading volumes. Clean spills immediately.
Dispose of used litmus papers and used test solutions properly. Do not pour vinegar or baking soda solutions down the sink in large amounts without checking school guidelines.

If evaporation is used in the performance task, learners use only sunlight or a warm place, never an open flame or hot plate. If the teacher demonstrates heating, learners stay an arm's length away, the teacher uses goggles and tongs or a heat-proof mat, and heating stops while a little liquid remains to avoid spitting hot salt.

days.title: Solute and Solvent in a Solution
days.objective: Learners will be able to identify the solute and solvent in common solutions by making and labelling a salt or sugar solution.
materials: 1 clear plastic cup or small glass beaker per group of 4-6 learners (8-10 groups for 40 learners), plus 2 extra cups for the sand/sugar comparison
1 large container of clean water (about 2 L) for refilling cups, or access to a tap
1 small bowl of table salt (about 100 g) with 12 plastic spoons
1 small bowl of white sugar (about 100 g) for the comparison, optional
1 small bowl of clean sand (about 100 g) for the non-dissolving comparison, optional
1 sheet of bond paper or a page in the science notebook per learner for drawing and labelling
12 pencils or ballpoint pens
1 roll of paper towels or clean rags for spills
1 trash bag for used cups and paper towels

flow.teacher: Greet the class and show the Day 1 title slide. Ask: 'When you stir sugar into water, where does the sugar go?' Let 3–4 learners answer; accept all ideas without correcting yet. Then show the question slide and ask: 'Have you ever seen sugar or salt disappear into water at home? What did the water look like after?' Take 2–3 answers (e.g., 'It looked clear', 'I could not see the sugar anymore'). Tell learners that today they will find out that the sugar or salt is still there, and they will learn the names of the two parts of a solution. Do not reveal the vocabulary yet.
flow.learners: Learners look at the slides, raise their hands to share experiences from home, and listen to classmates. In large classes, call on learners from different rows so more voices are heard.

flow.teacher: Show the purpose slide. Read the objective aloud: 'Today we will make a salt or sugar solution and label which part is the solute and which part is the solvent.' Tell learners that by the end of the lesson they must be able to look at any clear solution at home, like juice or salt water, and name the solute and solvent. Point out the success check: 'You can do this if you can label a drawing of your own cup correctly.'
flow.learners: Learners listen and read the objective on the slide. They may copy the objective in their notebooks if the teacher requires it.

flow.teacher: Show the vocabulary slide. Say each term and its meaning clearly, then have the class repeat the words 'solute' and 'solvent'. Explain: 'The solute is the substance that dissolves. The solvent is the substance that does the dissolving.' Give one example: 'In salt water, salt is the solute and water is the solvent.' Ask: 'If I dissolve sugar in water, which is the solute? [Sugar] Which is the solvent? [Water].' Next show the concept slide with the illustration of sugar dissolving; use it to explain that the particles spread evenly, so the mixture looks the same throughout. Safety reminder: 'We will not taste anything today. Keep hands away from your mouth and eyes, and wash hands after the activity.'
flow.learners: Learners repeat the terms, answer the teacher's questions aloud, and look at the illustration to see how particles spread.

flow.teacher: Show the activity slide and read the steps. Group learners into groups of 4-6. Give each group one cup, one spoon, access to water, and a small amount of salt (about one spoonful). Safety: 'If you use glass jars, they must stay on the table. If a jar breaks, do not pick up the pieces - call me. If you use plastic cups, still handle them carefully.' Instruct groups: (1) pour about half a cup of water, (2) add one spoonful of salt, (3) stir slowly and watch, (4) draw the cup and label salt as solute and water as solvent. Walk around and ask groups: 'Which substance disappeared from your eyes? [salt] Is it really gone? [No, it is spread in the water].' If time allows, let half the groups repeat with sugar and the other half try sand. After 10 minutes, show the reveal slide to check the labelling. Remind learners to wipe spills with paper towels and wash hands with soap after handling materials.
flow.learners: In groups of 4–6, learners pour water, add salt or sugar, stir, observe, and draw and label their cup on paper. They discuss within their group which substance is the solute and which is the solvent. One learner per group reports to the class.

flow.teacher: Show the summary slide. Ask the class: 'What makes a mixture a solution?' [It looks the same throughout, and the solute is spread evenly in the solvent]. Ask: 'What happens to sand in water?' [It does not dissolve; it settles at the bottom, so sand and water is not a solution]. Correct the common misconception: 'The solute does not disappear. It is still there, only its particles are too small to see and are spread evenly.' Have learners copy the summary lines into their notebooks.
flow.learners: Learners answer the questions, correct their own understanding, and copy the summary lines into their notebooks.

flow.teacher: Say: 'Close your notebooks. On a half sheet of paper, answer this exit ticket: In a glass of salt water, what is the solute and what is the solvent?' Give 3 minutes. Collect the papers. If time allows, ask 2 learners to share their answer. Remind learners not to taste any solution and to wash hands after the activity. Note: the correct answer is 'Salt is the solute; water is the solvent.' Common wrong answers: 8% means the learner divided by 100 instead of 200; 2% usually means they halved 4% or used 400 mL; 16% means they doubled instead of dividing.
flow.learners: Learners answer the exit ticket individually on paper and submit it. They clean their tables and wash hands if they handled materials.

expectedObservations: The salt or sugar seems to disappear from view, and the water stays clear.
After stirring, no solid salt or sugar is seen at the bottom of the cup.
Sand does not dissolve; it settles at the bottom and the water is not clear.
Learners can point to the salt as the solute and the water as the solvent in their labelled drawing.

check.question: In a glass of salt water, what is the solute and what is the solvent?
check.answer: Salt is the solute; water is the solvent.
check.why: Salt dissolves in water. The substance that dissolves is the solute, and the substance that does the dissolving is the solvent.

days.support: For learners who struggle, give them a labelled example drawing of a cup of salt water and ask them to copy it, then point to the salt and say 'solute' and to the water and say 'solvent'. Pair them with a stronger learner during the activity. Use a sentence frame: 'In my cup, ____ is the solute and ____ is the solvent.' Allow them to answer orally before writing.
days.extension: Ask learners who finish early to explain why a small glass and a big glass of equally sweet juice have about the same concentration, but the big glass contains more grams of sugar. Use 5 g/100 mL and 10 g/200 mL in your explanation. They should write two sentences with the word 'concentration'. They can also calculate the concentration if they add another 5 g of sugar to the 10% sugar solution to make 15 g in 100 mL [15%], and then predict whether more sugar could dissolve if the water were warmed.
days.longerPeriod: If the period is 50–60 minutes, add a 5–10 minute comparison of salt water, sugar water, and sand in water. Have each group prepare three small cups and draw all three side by side. Then hold a short class discussion on which mixtures are solutions and why sand is not. Use the extra time to let more groups report their labelled drawings and to correct misconceptions about the solute disappearing.

days.title: Measuring Concentration
days.objective: Learners will be able to express concentration as grams of solute per 100 mL of solution by measuring and calculating.
materials: 1 graduated cylinder (100 mL) per group of 4–6 learners
1 beaker or clear cup per group
tap water, about 200 mL per group
table salt, about 5 g per group (about 1 level teaspoon)
white sugar, about 10 g per group (about 2 level teaspoons)
1 small balance or weighing scale per group (or pre-weighed packets of 5 g salt and 10 g sugar)
1 stirring spoon or stirring rod per group
paper towels or clean cloth for spills
labelling tape or small sticky labels and a marker
learner notebooks and pencils
teacher's answer key for the practice calculation

flow.teacher: Greet the class and say that yesterday we learned to name the solute and the solvent. Ask the class: 'In a glass of salt water, which is the solute and which is the solvent?' [Salt is the solute; water is the solvent.] Show the Day 2 title slide and read the plan for today: we will measure how much solute is in a solution. Next, show the question slide and ask: 'Which glass of juice has more sugar dissolved in it: a small glass or a big glass, if both taste equally sweet?' Let 2–3 learners answer. Do not confirm yet; say we will find out what 'how much' really means. For a large class, ask learners to whisper their answer to a seatmate first, then call on two volunteers.
flow.learners: Learners recall solute and solvent from yesterday and answer the opening question. In pairs, they whisper their idea about which juice glass has more sugar, then two volunteers share with the class.

flow.teacher: State the goal in plain words: 'Today we will learn to say exactly how much solute is in a solution, using grams of solute per 100 millilitres of solution. We will also practise using the graduated cylinder correctly and safely.' Show the vocabulary slide and read each term aloud. Ask learners to repeat 'concentration' and 'percent mass per volume' after you. Explain that 'mass per volume' just means how many grams of solute are in a certain volume of solution. Tell them this number helps us compare solutions fairly, like comparing how strong one glass of juice is with another.
flow.learners: Learners listen, repeat the two new terms, and copy the vocabulary into their notebooks.

flow.teacher: Show the concept slide on concentration. Say: 'Concentration tells how much solute is in a certain amount of solution.' Give a simple example: if you put more sugar in the same glass of water, the solution is more concentrated. Then show the percent mass per volume slide. Write on the board: percent mass/volume = (grams of solute ÷ millilitres of solution) × 100. Work through one example slowly: 5 g salt in 100 mL solution gives (5 ÷ 100) × 100 = 5%. Ask: 'If we double the salt to 10 g in the same 100 mL, what is the percent?' [10%.] Next, show the graduated cylinder slide. Explain that a graduated cylinder measures volume more accurately than a beaker because its markings are finer. Demonstrate: place the cylinder on a flat table, pour water, then bend down so your eye is level with the liquid surface and read the bottom of the curved surface (the meniscus). Ask two learners to come up and read a volume aloud. Safety: glass cylinders can break; carry them with two hands, never use a cracked one, and wipe spills at once so no one slips.
flow.learners: Learners follow the worked example, answer the doubling question, and watch the teacher demonstrate reading a graduated cylinder. Two volunteers practise reading the volume at eye level.

flow.teacher: Show the activity slide and read the steps. Organize groups of 4-6. Give each group a graduated cylinder, a cup, water, a balance or pre-weighed packets, salt, sugar, a spoon, a label, and an equipment handling checklist. Say: 'First, put 5 g of salt in the cup. Add about 60 mL of water and stir until it dissolves. Pour the solution into the graduated cylinder (placed on a flat surface) and add water until the bottom of the meniscus reaches the 100 mL mark. Pour this solution back into the cup and label it: salt solution, 5 g per 100 mL of solution. Repeat with 10 g of sugar in a separate cup, again making the final volume 100 mL. Record the mass of solute (5 g and 10 g) and the final volume (100 mL) on your record sheet, and check the equipment handling checklist: cylinder on flat surface, eye level at bottom of meniscus, carried with two hands.' Walk around and check that groups read the cylinder at eye level and that they record the mass and the volume. Ask groups: 'Which solution is more concentrated, the salt or the sugar one?' [The sugar one: 10% compared with 5%.] Safety: do not taste any solution; wash hands with soap and water after handling; handle glass cylinders carefully; clean spills immediately. Tell learners they may pour the used solutions down the sink with plenty of water only if your school allows it; otherwise collect them in a labelled container.
flow.learners: In groups of 4–6, learners dissolve 5 g of salt in about 60 mL of water, then make the solution up to 100 mL in a graduated cylinder and label it. They repeat with 10 g of sugar, making the final volume 100 mL. Each learner records the mass of solute, the volume of solution, and the calculated percent mass/volume in a table, and completes the equipment handling checklist. Groups compare their two solutions and decide which is more concentrated.

flow.teacher: Show the check slide. Read the question and the four choices. Give learners 60 seconds to think, then ask them to raise one finger for A, two for B, three for C, four for D. Do not say the answer yet. Then show the reveal slide and explain: 8 g sugar in 200 mL gives 8 ÷ 200 = 0.04, and 0.04 × 100 = 4%. Ask: 'Why do we divide by the volume of the solution, not by the amount of water?' [Because concentration describes the solution as a whole.] Then ask the class to say in one sentence what concentration means. [How much solute is in a certain amount of solution.] Summarize the formula on the board.
flow.learners: Learners choose an answer by holding up fingers, then check their thinking against the reveal. They explain why the volume of the solution is used, and one learner states the meaning of concentration in a full sentence.

flow.teacher: Show the summary slide and give learners one minute to copy the formula and its meaning. Then give the exit ticket on paper: 'If you dissolve 8 g of sugar in water to make 200 mL of solution, what is the concentration in percent mass/volume?' Learners answer on a half-sheet of paper and show their work. Remind them not to call out. Collect the papers. If time allows, ask two learners to show their working on the board. The expected answer is 4%: 8 ÷ 200 = 0.04, then 0.04 × 100 = 4%. Common wrong answers: 8% means the learner divided by 100 instead of the actual volume; 2% means they divided 200 by 8 and made an error. Note these for tomorrow's review. Remind everyone to wash hands after handling the salt and sugar and to return the glassware to the shelf carefully.
flow.learners: Learners copy the summary, then answer the exit ticket on paper, showing the mass, the volume, and the calculation. They hand in their papers and help return the materials.

expectedObservations: The salt and sugar both seem to disappear, but the solution is still there; the solute has spread evenly through the water.
Both salt and sugar dissolve completely when stirred; neither is visible afterwards. We did not control grain size, so we cannot compare how fast salt and sugar dissolve.
The 10 g sugar in 100 mL of solution gives 10% mass/volume, which is more concentrated than the 5% salt solution.
Learners reading the graduated cylinder at eye level get a volume close to 100 mL; reading from above or below gives a different value.

check.question: If you dissolve 8 g of sugar in water to make 200 mL of solution, what is the concentration in % mass/volume?
check.why: 8 g divided by 200 mL is 0.04. Multiply by 100 to convert to percent: 0.04 × 100 = 4%.

days.support: For learners who struggle with the calculation, give a worked template: mass of solute = ___ g, volume of solution = ___ mL, then mass ÷ volume = ___, then × 100 = ___ %. Let them use a calculator if available. Pair them with a learner who has finished and ask them to explain each step aloud. If measuring equipment is limited, use pre-weighed packets of 5 g salt and 10 g sugar so the focus stays on the calculation, and read the volume from a pre-filled 100 mL cylinder.
days.extension: Ask learners to calculate the concentration if they add another 5 g of sugar to the 10% sugar solution to make 15 g in 100 mL [15%], and then predict whether more sugar could dissolve if the water were warmed. They can also write two sentences explaining why a small glass and a big glass of equally sweet juice do not necessarily have the same concentration.
days.longerPeriod: If the period runs 50–60 minutes, add a comparison task: groups prepare a 5% sugar solution and a 10% sugar solution, then line up all cups from lightest to most concentrated and explain their order. Also add a short demonstration of reading the graduated cylinder from above, at, and below eye level to show how the reading changes, and discuss why reading at eye level is best.

days.title: Heat and Dissolving
days.objective: Learners will demonstrate that warm water dissolves a greater maximum amount of salt than cold water, and distinguish this from dissolving faster.
materials: 2 clear plastic cups per group of 4–6 learners (about 20 cups for a class of 40)
Salt, about 2 teaspoons per group (or sugar, if salt is unavailable)
Warm water (not boiling) in a jug, about 200 mL per group
Cold water (room temperature or chilled) in a jug, about 200 mL per group
1 teaspoon per group for adding solute
1 stirrer or spoon per group
1 stopwatch or phone timer per group (teacher may time the whole class)
Manila paper or notebook for recording observations
Masking tape and marker for labelling cups C (cold) and W (warm)

flow.teacher: Greet the class and remind them of yesterday's lesson: they measured concentration as grams of solute per 100 mL of solution. Ask: 'When you make a glass of juice or coffee at home, which dissolves faster — the powder in cold water or in warm water?' Let 2–3 learners answer. Accept all answers without judging. Say: 'Today we will test this with salt and water.' Show the day slide with today's title.
flow.learners: Recall yesterday's concentration work. Answer the warm-up question aloud or by raising hands. Listen to the day's goal.

flow.teacher: Read the objective aloud: 'Today we will show that heat speeds up the dissolving of a solid solute in water.' Explain that learners will compare cold and warm water using the same amount of salt. Ask: 'What will we change? What will we keep the same?' Guide them to say: change the water temperature, keep the amount of salt, the amount of water, and the stirring the same. Show the question slide to set up the investigation.
flow.learners: Listen to the objective. Suggest what to change and what to keep the same in the test.

flow.teacher: Introduce the three key ideas with the concept slides. First: warm water makes many solid solutes dissolve faster. Second: stirring speeds up dissolving but does not change how much can dissolve. Third: there is a limit to how much solute can dissolve at a given temperature, and warm water can often dissolve a greater maximum amount of solid solute than cold water. Ask: 'If I stir harder, will I be able to dissolve more salt than before?' Expected answer: no, stirring only makes it faster; the maximum depends on the solute, solvent, and temperature. Correct the common wrong answer that stirring increases solubility. Show the vocabulary slide for solubility and give the simple meaning: the most solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature. Explain that today we will compare the maximum amount of salt that can dissolve in cold and warm water.
flow.learners: Listen and answer the teacher's questions. Copy the meaning of solubility into their notebooks.

flow.teacher: Before the activity, give the safety reminder clearly: 'Do not taste or drink the salt water. Warm water only - not boiling. The teacher will check the water temperature before you start. If water spills, wipe it at once so nobody slips.' Show the activity slide. Organise groups of 4-6. Each group gets two cups labelled C and W, a graduated cylinder or marked cup, a teaspoon, stirrer, salt, and cold and warm water. First, have learners measure 100 mL of cold water into cup C and 100 mL of warm water into cup W. Then add one teaspoon of salt to each cup at the same time and stir both cups at the same steady rate until no more dissolves. Keep adding salt one teaspoon at a time, stirring after each addition, until solid remains undissolved. Record the number of teaspoons that dissolved in each cup. Teacher circulates and asks: 'Which cup dissolved more salt? Which cup dissolved faster?' Expected: warm water dissolved more salt and faster. Remind learners not to pour the cups out until you say so.
flow.learners: In groups of 4–6, label cups C and W, measure 100 mL into each, add salt one teaspoon at a time, stir both cups at the same steady rate, and record how many teaspoons dissolved before solid remained. Compare the two totals.

flow.teacher: Show the check slide. Read the question and the four choices. Give 30 seconds for learners to think, then ask them to raise the card or hand sign for their answer (1 finger for A, 2 for B, 3 for C, 4 for D). Note who chooses the wrong answer. Show the reveal slide and discuss: warm water particles move faster and hit the sugar particles more often, so the sugar dissolves more quickly. Also, warm water can dissolve a greater maximum amount of sugar than cold water. Address the wrong answer: a learner who picks cold water may be thinking of keeping juice cold, but cold slows dissolving; it does not speed it up.
flow.learners: Answer the check question individually. Show their answer with hand signs. Listen to the explanation and correct their thinking.

flow.teacher: Ask the class to build the big idea together: 'What did we prove today about heat and dissolving?' Expected: heat makes many solid solutes dissolve faster and can also dissolve more. Ask: 'Did stirring change how much salt could dissolve, or only how fast?' Expected: only how fast. Say: 'Remember, there is a limit to how much can dissolve at a given temperature, and warm water has a higher limit in our test. Warm water dissolved more salt and faster.' Show the summary slide and have learners copy the lines.
flow.learners: Answer the teacher's questions. Copy the summary lines into their notebooks.

flow.teacher: Give the exit-ticket question on paper: 'In which water will a teaspoon of sugar dissolve faster: cold or warm? Which water can dissolve more sugar overall?' Learners answer in one or two lines and write one sentence of explanation. Collect the papers. Expected answer: warm water dissolves sugar faster and can dissolve more sugar overall, because warm water particles move faster and hit the sugar particles more often, and warm water has a higher solubility limit for sugar. Use the results to decide who needs support tomorrow.
flow.learners: Write their answer and one-sentence explanation on a small paper. Submit to the teacher.

expectedObservations: More teaspoons of salt dissolve in warm water than in cold water before solid remains undissolved.
Stirring at the same rate helps both cups dissolve quickly, but the maximum amount in warm water is greater.
In both cups, solid salt remains at the bottom after saturation; more undissolved salt remains in the cold cup.
Some learners may see undissolved salt at the bottom; this is the saturation point, and it is expected and recorded.

check.question: In which water will a teaspoon of sugar dissolve faster: cold or warm? Which water can dissolve more sugar?
check.answer: Warm water dissolves sugar faster and can dissolve more sugar overall.
check.why: Warm water particles move faster and collide with sugar particles more often, pulling them into solution more quickly. Warm water also has a higher solubility limit for sugar, so more can dissolve.

days.support: For learners who struggle, pair them with a stronger learner in the group and give them a simple role: holding the timer or drawing the two cups. Provide a sentence starter for the exit ticket: 'The sugar dissolves faster in ____ water because ____.' Re-read the key idea aloud and ask them to repeat it back.
days.extension: For learners who finish early, ask them to design a test to find out whether stirring changes the amount of salt that can dissolve. They should list their materials, what they will change, what they will keep the same, and what they expect to see.
days.longerPeriod: If the period runs 50–60 minutes, add a second round where groups repeat the test with sugar instead of salt and compare whether the result is the same. Use the extra time to discuss why warm water dissolves faster using the particle model: faster-moving water particles hit the solute particles more often.

days.title: Testing with Litmus
days.objective: Learners will be able to classify common solutions as acids, bases, or salts using litmus paper.
materials: red and blue litmus paper, cut into small strips (about 40 of each color)
vinegar (about 100 mL), calamansi juice (about 100 mL), baking soda solution (about 5 g in 250 mL water), and table salt solution (about 5 g in 250 mL water), each in a labelled bottle or cup
4 small clear cups or saucers per group for holding the test solutions
clean spoons or droppers (4 per group) and 1 beaker of clean water for rinsing
waste cup or small bin for used litmus papers (1 per group)
lab apron or old shirt, plus water and soap for handwashing
record table printout or drawing per learner: solution name, red litmus result, blue litmus result, classification
chalkboard or manila paper for the class summary table
teacher's copy of safety rules and the answer key

flow.teacher: Begin by showing the first slide, Day 4: Testing with Litmus. Say that today we will find out a way scientists test whether a liquid is an acid, a base, or a salt. Then show 'What Do You Think?' and ask: Think about calamansi juice you have tasted in food at home — what flavour was it? (sour). Ask: What do you think makes sour foods sour? Accept all answers without judging. Tell the class that in science we do not judge by taste alone; we use a test paper. Show 'Litmus Paper' and explain that litmus is a special paper made from a natural dye; it changes color when it touches acids or bases. Ask: Why is it safer to use litmus paper than to taste a liquid? (Because we do not know if it is safe; some liquids are harmful.) Then move to the lesson purpose. Management for large classes: ask learners to sit in groups of 4–6 with materials already prepared; keep the class in listening mode for this part.
flow.learners: Learners answer the questions aloud or with a quick show of hands. They listen and observe the litmus strips. In pairs, they share one idea about what makes sour foods sour.

flow.teacher: State today's goal in plain words: 'By the end of this lesson, you will be able to classify common solutions as acids, bases, or salts using litmus paper, and you will practice proper handling of this science equipment.' Write the words acid, base, salt, litmus, neutral on the board as a word bank. Show 'How Litmus Reacts' and read the two rules together with the class. Use a choral reading: 'Acids turn blue litmus red. Bases turn red litmus blue.' Ask two learners to repeat the rules in their own words. Tell learners they will get a set of four solutions to test and must record their results like real scientists.
flow.learners: Learners listen, copy the word bank into their notebooks, and repeat the two litmus rules. Two volunteers restate the rules.

flow.teacher: Show 'Our Four Test Solutions' and name each solution aloud: vinegar, calamansi juice, baking soda solution, table salt solution. Ask: Do not taste; tell me what you already know about these liquids. (Vinegar and calamansi are sour; baking soda is used in baking; salt we eat.) Accept answers, then say we will not assume; we will test. Show 'Safety First' and read each rule. Stress: no tasting, wash hands after, do not splash liquids on skin or eyes, keep litmus strips on the table not near the mouth. Tell learners the teacher will place small amounts into cups; learners will not pour from bottles. Safety instruction for this step: the teacher pours the four solutions into labelled cups for each group before learners handle them; if a learner spills anything, they should ask the teacher with a hand raised, not wipe it with bare hands. Then show 'Activity: Test Each Solution' and demonstrate one test with red litmus paper: tear a small strip, dip it into vinegar, wait 5 seconds, place on the record sheet, and note the color. Remind them to use a new strip for each solution and each paper color. Class management: teacher walks from group to group during the activity; the record keeper writes, the materials manager handles strips, the reporter will share results. Safety reminder repeated: litmus paper is not to be eaten; used papers go in the waste cup, not the floor.
flow.learners: Learners work in groups of 4–6. The materials manager gets strips, the tester dips each strip, the recorder writes the color in the table, and the reporter prepares to share. They test all four solutions with both red and blue litmus paper. They place used papers in the waste cup.

flow.teacher: Bring the class back together after the activity. Show 'What Results Should We Compare?' and ask groups to share their recorded colors one by one. As they report, fill in a class table on the board: solution, red litmus, blue litmus, classification. Ask: Which solutions turned blue litmus red? (vinegar and calamansi juice). What does that tell us? (They are acids). Which solution turned red litmus blue? (baking soda solution). What is a solution that is a base? (baking soda solution is a common base). Which solution did not change either paper? (table salt solution, and sugar water is also neutral). Explain: Litmus tells us acid or base only. A no-change result means neutral, not 'it is a salt' — sugar water is neutral too. Some salts, like baking soda, actually give a basic solution. Remind learners: 'Do not use one result to guess another; report what you saw. If your strip did not change, the solution is neutral.'
flow.learners: Pairs or group reporters read their tables aloud. The class listens and compares their group's results with the board table. Learners correct their own tables if they disagree with the evidence and can explain why.

flow.teacher: Show the exit-ticket question slide and read it once: 'Red litmus paper is dipped into vinegar. What happens?' Tell learners to copy and answer on a half-sheet of paper. Say: no talking, 3 minutes. After collecting, or asking learners to hold up their paper, go over the answer using the reveal slide: red litmus stays red in an acid, because acids turn blue litmus red. Emphasize: red litmus paper changing color indicates a base (it turns blue), so vinegar, an acid, will not change red litmus. If answers are wrong, ask: Which paper changes in an acid? (blue litmus changes to red). Remind class that blue litmus turns red with acids, and red litmus turns blue with bases. Before dismissing, collect materials and instruct handwashing with soap and water. Safety check: ensure all used litmus papers are in the waste cup and solutions are capped.
flow.learners: Each learner writes the answer to the exit-ticket question individually on paper. They submit or show their answer. They wash hands and help clean their table area.

expectedObservations: Vinegar turns blue litmus paper red and does not change red litmus paper.
Calamansi juice turns blue litmus paper red and does not change red litmus paper.
Baking soda solution turns red litmus paper blue and does not change blue litmus paper.
Table salt solution does not change the color of either red or blue litmus paper and is neutral (a salt solution).
Sugar water, if tested, also does not change either litmus color and is neutral.
The color changes for acids and bases are clear enough to see on the strips; the strips may change back a bit if left wet for a long time, so read the color within a few seconds.

check.question: Red litmus paper is dipped into vinegar. What happens to it?
check.why: Vinegar is an acid, and acids turn blue litmus paper red. They do not turn red litmus paper blue (that shows a base).

days.support: For learners who struggle, give them a pre-printed table with the four solution names already written. Demonstrate one strip test in front of them. Pair them with a stronger peer as a buddy, but ask each learner to record one row themselves. Use a simple color card: red on one side, blue on the other. Ask them to point to the color they see before writing. Provide the sentence frame: 'The red litmus turned ___ when I tested ___ . This means the solution is ___ .' Reassure learners that observing carefully is the main goal, not memorizing all words at once.
days.extension: Groups who finish early can plan a safe test of two more common liquids at home or in school, such as sugar water or a little calamansi juice mixed with water, and predict whether the liquid will turn blue litmus red, turn red litmus blue, or stay the same. They write their prediction and why. They may also sort the four solutions into a simple table showing acid, base, and neutral, and explain one everyday use for each. For example, vinegar is used in cooking; baking soda is used in cleaning and baking; salt is used in food. They do not taste or use strong cleaning chemicals. (Teacher note: Vinegar and calamansi juice are both weak acids; strength is not tested by litmus.)
days.longerPeriod: If the school runs 50–60 minute periods, add 5–10 minutes to the activity phase so learners can test sugar water as a fifth neutral solution and compare it with salt solution. Use the extra time to let each group report their full table and to discuss why salt solution counts as neutral while baking soda and vinegar change litmus. Add a short teacher demonstration: test a very small amount of calamansi juice diluted in water and compare the color of blue litmus with undiluted calamansi juice, explaining that color intensity may vary but the direction of change is the same. Keep all safety rules in place and do not add strong acids or bases.

days.title: Review and Assess: Solutions Week
days.objective: Learners will be able to review and apply solute/solvent identification, concentration calculation, solubility factors, litmus classification, and safe equipment use in a written assessment and a performance task plan.
materials: 1 written assessment paper per learner (7 items covering solute/solvent, concentration, solubility factors, litmus, and safety, plus a performance task)
1 answer sheet per learner
1 performance task planning sheet per group of 4–6 learners
manila paper and markers for group plans (1 set per group)
chalkboard or whiteboard for listing safety rules
teacher's answer key for the written assessment

flow.teacher: Begin with a quick whole-class recall. Ask: 'What are the two parts of a solution?' (solute and solvent). 'Give one example of each from our lessons.' (salt is the solute, water is the solvent). Show the day slide and the question slide. Say: 'Today we review everything we learned this week about solutions, then you will plan your own investigation.' Keep the pace brisk; take 3–4 answers only. For large classes, have learners whisper the answer to a seatmate before calling on two or three.
flow.learners: Learners answer aloud or whisper to a partner, then listen as the teacher confirms the definitions.

flow.teacher: State the goal clearly: 'Today you will show what you know about solutions in a short written assessment, then in groups you will plan a safe investigation to find how much salt is dissolved in 100 mL of salt water.' Show the purpose slide and read the three outcomes aloud. Remind learners that the assessment is individual and quiet.
flow.learners: Learners listen and read the outcomes on the slide.

flow.teacher: Distribute the assessment papers and answer sheets face down. Say: 'You have 18 minutes. Work quietly on your own. Read each item carefully.' Set a visible timer. Walk around to keep order; do not give answers. For large classes, assign one learner per row to collect papers at the end. If a learner asks for help, say: 'Do your best; we will review after.' Collect all papers when time is up.
flow.learners: Learners complete the written assessment individually and silently, then pass their papers to the row collector.

flow.teacher: Now move to the group planning task. Show the activity slide. Read the steps aloud: list materials; write safe steps (evaporate the water, weigh the remaining salt); show how to calculate concentration in percent mass per volume. Before groups start writing, run the one-minute check on d5s6: read the four choices, take answers from two groups, then reveal d5s7 and ask groups to check their plan uses that rule. Remind them: 'Do not taste anything. Handle glass graduated cylinders carefully. Learners do not use heat sources; if evaporation is needed, place the dish in direct sunlight or a warm, well-ventilated area. If the teacher demonstrates heating, learners stay an arm's length away, the teacher uses goggles and tongs or a heat-proof mat, and heating stops while a little liquid remains to avoid spitting hot salt.' Give groups 8 minutes to write their plan on manila paper, and tell them to include an equipment handling checklist for the measurements they will take. Then ask two groups to share one safety rule each. Write the rules on the board.
flow.learners: In groups of 4–6, learners plan the investigation on manila paper. They list materials, write safe numbered steps, and write the concentration formula. Two groups share one safety rule with the class.

flow.teacher: Guide the class to summarize the week. Show the summary slide. Ask: 'What is a solution?' (a mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent). 'How do we express concentration?' (grams of solute per 100 mL of solution, or percent mass per volume). 'What changes how fast a solute dissolves?' (heat and stirring speed it up; heat also often increases solubility). 'What does litmus tell us?' (Acids turn blue litmus red; bases turn red litmus blue; no change means neutral — not that it is a salt. Some salts, like baking soda, give a basic solution.) Have learners copy the summary lines.
flow.learners: Learners answer the questions aloud and copy the summary lines into their notebooks.

flow.teacher: Show the check slide. Read the question: 'What is one safety rule when using a graduated cylinder?' Let learners choose from the four options. Then reveal the correct answer. Ask one learner to explain why reading at eye level matters. Finally, give the exit ticket on a small piece of paper: 'You dissolve 6 g of salt in water to make 150 mL of solution. What is the concentration in % mass/volume? Show your work.' Collect the exit tickets as learners leave. The answer is 4% because 6 ÷ 150 = 0.04, and 0.04 × 100 = 4%.
flow.learners: Learners answer the check question, discuss the reason, then write and submit the exit ticket on a small slip of paper.

expectedObservations: Learners correctly identify salt as the solute and water as the solvent in salt water.
Learners calculate concentration by dividing grams of solute by milliliters of solution and multiplying by 100.
Learners state that warm water makes a solid solute dissolve faster than cold water.
Learners classify vinegar and calamansi juice as acids (blue litmus turns red) and baking soda solution as a base (red litmus turns blue).
Learners describe a salt solution as neutral and say it does not change litmus color.
Learners list at least one safe practice for handling glassware or chemicals.

check.question: You dissolve 6 g of salt in water to make 150 mL of solution. What is the concentration in % mass/volume?
check.why: 6 g divided by 150 mL is 0.04. Multiply by 100 to convert to percent: 0.04 × 100 = 4%.

days.support: For learners who struggle with the calculation, give a worked example: 5 g in 100 mL is 5 ÷ 100 = 0.05, then 0.05 × 100 = 5%. Provide a multiplication table for 100 and allow them to use a calculator if available. For the planning task, give a partially completed plan with blanks for materials and steps. Pair them with a stronger learner during group work, and check their formula before they write it on manila paper.
days.extension: Ask learners who finish early to write a second plan: how would they test whether stirring changes how much salt can dissolve? They should state their prediction, the variables to keep the same, and how they will measure. Or ask them to calculate the concentration of a solution made with 12 g of sugar in 300 mL of solution (4%).
days.longerPeriod: If the period runs 50–60 minutes, add 5–10 minutes for groups to present their full investigation plan to the class, with one group giving feedback on another group's safety steps. Also allow time to review two or three written assessment items as a class and discuss common errors.

assessment.prompt: In a glass of salt water, which substance is the solute?
assessment.explanation: The solute is the substance that dissolves. In salt water, salt dissolves in water, so salt is the solute. Water is the solvent. Glass and air are not part of the solution.

assessment.prompt: A learner dissolves 8 grams of sugar in water to make 200 mL of solution. What is the concentration in % mass/volume?
assessment.explanation: Percent mass/volume = (mass of solute in grams ÷ volume of solution in mL) × 100. 8 g ÷ 200 mL = 0.04. 0.04 × 100 = 4%. The other choices come from common errors: using 8 directly as percent (8%), doubling the correct answer (16%), or dividing by 400 mL (2%).

assessment.prompt: A student wants to make sugar dissolve faster in water without changing the maximum amount that can eventually dissolve. Which action should the student take?
assessment.explanation: Stirring increases the rate of dissolving but does not change the solubility limit. Using hotter water increases both the rate and usually the maximum amount that can dissolve. Adding more sugar or using less water changes the ratio of solute to solvent but does not speed up dissolving.

assessment.prompt: Which household solution turns red litmus paper blue?
assessment.explanation: Baking soda solution is a base. Bases turn red litmus paper blue. Vinegar and calamansi juice are acids, which turn blue litmus red. Salt water is a neutral solution and generally does not change the color of litmus.

assessment.prompt: You need to measure 45 mL of water accurately. Which piece of equipment should you use instead of a beaker?
assessment.explanation: A graduated cylinder is designed for accurate volume measurement. A beaker has approximate markings and is better for holding, mixing, or pouring. A stirring rod does not measure volume. An Erlenmeyer flask is used for heating or mixing and its markings are not precise.

assessment.prompt: A learner dissolves 15 g of table salt in water to make 500 mL of solution. Calculate the concentration in % mass/volume. Show your work.
assessment.explanation: Percent mass/volume is grams of solute per 100 mL of solution. 15 g of salt in 500 mL gives 0.03 g/mL. Multiplying by 100 gives 3 g per 100 mL, which is 3%.

assessment.prompt: Design an investigation to determine the amount of salt dissolved in 100 mL of salt water. Your plan must include: a research question, a list of materials, safe steps using evaporation to separate salt from water, and how you will calculate the concentration in % mass/volume. Also, include an equipment handling checklist for the measurements you will take.
assessment.answer: Sample plan: Question: How many grams of salt are dissolved in 100 mL of salt water? Materials: 100 mL salt water sample, shallow dish, graduated cylinder, balance, heat source or sunny area. Steps: Measure 100 mL of salt water in a graduated cylinder. Pour into a clean, dry dish. Weigh the empty dish first. Evaporate the water by gentle heating or leaving in sunlight. Weigh the dish with the remaining salt. Subtract the empty dish mass to find salt mass. Calculate concentration: (mass of salt ÷ 100 mL) × 100 = % mass/volume. Safety: Use low heat, handle dish with care, wash hands after.
assessment.explanation: The plan should show understanding of evaporation to separate solute and solvent, accurate measurement of volume and mass, safe handling, and the concentration formula. This task assesses solute-solvent identification, quantitative concentration, and proper use of equipment.

slides.title: What Dissolves? Solute, Solvent, and Safety
lines: Grade 7 Science · Term 1 · Week 6
Five 45-minute lessons
slides.notes: How to use this deck: each lesson starts with a "Day" slide. Speaker notes under every slide tell you what to say, what to ask and the answers to expect; they show only in Presenter View, never on the TV. Question slides come before their answer slides, so learners can think before the answer appears. The teacher guide (separate PDF) explains the science behind the week, common wrong ideas, and the full answer key.

slides.title: Day 1: Solute and Solvent
lines: Today: We will make a salt or sugar solution and name its parts.
slides.notes: Greet the class warmly and show this slide as learners settle down. Read the line aloud. Say: 'Today we will find out what happens when salt or sugar is mixed with water.' Keep this short, about 1 minute. Do not explain solute and solvent yet; the goal is to set the day's purpose. Ask: 'Who has helped mix sugar into water at home?' Take a few answers to connect the lesson to their daily life. This slide is a starting point, not a test.

slides.title: Where does the sugar go?
lines: When you stir sugar into water, where does the sugar go?
slides.notes: Ask the question and let 3–4 learners answer. Expected answers: 'It disappears', 'It melts', 'It goes to the bottom', 'It mixes with water'. Do not judge any answer yet. Say: 'Keep your idea in mind. By the end of the lesson, we will check if your idea is correct.' If a learner says 'It disappears', reply: 'That is what many people think. Let us find out today if it really disappears.' This builds curiosity and helps you later correct the misconception that the solute vanishes.

slides.title: What we will learn today
lines: Make a salt or sugar solution.
Label the solute and the solvent.
Be able to name the parts of any solution.
slides.notes: Read the objective in learner-friendly words. Say: 'By the end of 45 minutes, you should be able to look at a clear glass of salt water and say which part is the solute and which part is the solvent.' Tell learners that the solute and solvent are the two parts of every solution. Ask: 'Are you ready to make your own solution?' This slide sets the success check for the lesson. Keep it to about 2 minutes. If learners look confused, say: 'We will learn the words in a moment; first, let us know our goal.'

slides.title: Three words to learn
lines: solute — the substance that dissolves
solvent — the substance that does the dissolving
solution — a mixture that looks the same throughout
slides.notes: Read each term and meaning slowly. Have the class repeat 'solute' and 'solvent' after you. Give a concrete example: 'In salt water, salt is the solute and water is the solvent.' Ask: 'If I dissolve sugar in water, which is the solute? [Sugar] Which is the solvent? [Water].' Correct pronunciation gently. Remind learners that 'solution' is the whole mixture, not just the solute or the solvent. Tell them they will see these words again in the activity. Safety reminder: 'We will not taste anything today.' Keep the pace quick but clear, about 4 minutes.

slides.title: The solute spreads through the solvent
lines: When a solute dissolves, its particles spread evenly in the solvent.
The mixture looks the same throughout.
The solute is still there, even if you cannot see it.

image.alt: A hand-drawn glass containing liquid with evenly distributed tiny dots representing particles suspended throughout.

slides.notes: Use the drawing to explain what happens at the particle level, but keep it simple. Say: 'The sugar breaks into very tiny pieces called particles. These particles spread out evenly among the water particles. That is why the water looks clear and the sugar seems to disappear.' Ask: 'If the sugar is still there, why can we not see it?' [The particles are too small and spread out]. Correct the misconception: 'Do not say the sugar disappeared. It is still there.' This is the key idea of the day. Spend about 4 minutes.

slides.title: Make your own solution
lines: 1. Pour about half a cup of water.
2. Add one spoonful of salt.
3. Stir slowly and watch.
4. Draw the cup and label the solute and the solvent.

image.alt: A spoon pouring granular solid (appearing as sugar or salt) into a glass of water, with particles shown falling and some submerged in the liquid.

slides.notes: Read the steps aloud. Group learners into 4-6 and give each group one cup, one spoon, water, and a small amount of salt. Safety: 'If you use glass jars, they must stay on the table. If a jar breaks, do not pick up the pieces - call me. If you use plastic cups, still handle them carefully. Do not taste anything. Wash hands with soap after.' Tell learners to draw the cup and label it. Walk around and ask: 'Which is the solute? Which is the solvent?' Expected: salt is the solute, water is the solvent. If a group says the salt disappeared, say: 'Look at the water. It looks clear and the same throughout, but the salt is still there, spread as tiny particles.' Give 10 minutes.

slides.title: Why is sand not a solution?
lines: Sand does not dissolve in water.
It settles at the bottom.
A solution looks the same throughout, like salt water.
slides.notes: If some groups tested sand, ask them to describe what they saw. Expected: 'The sand stayed at the bottom and the water was not clear.' Explain that in a solution, the solute spreads evenly and the mixture looks the same throughout. Sand does not dissolve, so sand and water is a mixture but not a solution. Ask: 'Is salt water a solution? Why?' [Yes, because the salt spreads evenly and the water looks the same throughout]. This helps learners distinguish solutions from other mixtures. Use 3–4 minutes.

slides.title: Salt water: which is the solute?
lines: In a glass of salt water, what is the solute?
slides.notes: Ask the class to choose without shouting out. Give 30 seconds. Then ask one learner to answer and another to explain why. Do not reveal the answer yet; the next slide gives the correct answer. If many choose 'Water', that is a sign they confuse the solute and the solvent. After the reveal, ask: 'Which one is the solvent then?' [Water]. Keep this quick so learners stay focused before the summary. This check tests the day's main idea, not memory of a fact from earlier.

slides.title: Answer: Salt is the solute
lines: Salt is the solute; water is the solvent.
The solute is the substance that dissolves.
slides.notes: Reveal and explain: 'Salt is the solute because it dissolves. Water is the solvent because it does the dissolving.' Connect back to the activity: 'In your own cup, the salt was the solute and the water was the solvent.' If any group labelled it the other way, have them correct their drawing now. Ask again: 'What is the solute in sugar water?' [Sugar]. This is the moment to fix the confusion. Spend about 2 minutes. Then move to the summary so learners copy the key idea.

slides.title: What we learned today
lines: A solution looks the same throughout.
The solute is the substance that dissolves.
The solvent is the substance that does the dissolving.
In salt water, salt is the solute and water is the solvent.
slides.notes: Read the summary lines aloud and have learners copy them into their notebooks. Emphasise the sentence 'In salt water, salt is the solute and water is the solvent.' Correct any remaining misconception by saying: 'The solute does not disappear; it spreads in tiny particles.' Ask one or two learners to give another example, such as sugar in water, and identify the solute and solvent. Tell learners they will use these words again in the next lessons. Remind them to clean up and wash hands after handling materials. This slide prepares them for the exit ticket.

slides.title: Day 2: Measuring Concentration
lines: Today: we will measure how much solute is in a solution and write it as a percent.
slides.notes: Read the title and the plan aloud in a calm, friendly voice. Tell learners that yesterday we named the solute and solvent, and today we will put a number on 'how much'. Say the goal in your own words: we will learn to express concentration as grams of solute per 100 millilitres of solution. Ask learners to keep their notebooks open and ready for a short table of measurements. Timing: about 1 minute. No safety reminder needed yet, but say that we will handle glass and food materials later, so we will wash hands and be careful.

slides.title: Which juice has more sugar?
lines: A small glass and a big glass of juice taste equally sweet. Which one has more sugar dissolved in it?
slides.notes: This question activates prior knowledge from Day 1 and hooks interest. Let learners whisper their answer to a seatmate for 20 seconds, then call on two or three volunteers. Accept different answers without judging. If a learner says the big glass, ask: 'Why do you think so?' The point is not to settle it yet but to show that 'how much' is hard to compare without measuring. Say we will learn a fair way to say exactly how much solute is in a solution. Expected answers: the big glass, because there is more juice; or the same, because they taste the same. Do not reveal any answer; the idea comes later.

slides.title: Words we will use today
lines: concentration — the amount of solute in a certain amount of solution
percent mass per volume — grams of solute in 100 mL of solution
graduated cylinder — a tall glass tool that measures liquid volume

image.alt: A hand-drawn glass containing a liquid with undissolved granular solid settled at the bottom and some floating on top, suggesting excess solute in a solution.

slides.notes: Read each term and its meaning slowly. Ask the class to repeat 'concentration' and 'percent mass per volume' after you. Explain that 'mass per volume' just means grams of solute in a certain volume of solution. Point out that the graduated cylinder has fine markings so it measures better than a beaker. Tell learners to copy these three words into their notebooks. Emphasize that concentration is about the solution as a whole, not just the water. Timing: about 2 minutes. No safety reminder needed for this slide.

slides.title: What concentration tells us
lines: Concentration tells how much solute is in a certain amount of solution.
More solute in the same amount of solution means a more concentrated solution.

image.alt: A hand-drawn glass containing a liquid with granular solid material settled at the bottom and some floating or suspended near the top, suggesting undissolved solute in a solution.

slides.notes: Use the drawing to show the difference between a solution with more dissolved particles and one with fewer. Say that both glasses may contain the same kind of solute, but the one with more particles has more solute in the same amount of solution. Ask: 'If I add water to the glass with more particles, will it become more or less concentrated?' [Less concentrated.] This helps learners see that concentration depends on both the amount of solute and the amount of solution. Note: Colour only helps for coloured solutes like juice. Salt and sugar solutions stay clear at any concentration — we must calculate. Keep it short: about 2 minutes. No safety reminder needed.

slides.title: Percent mass per volume
lines: Percent mass per volume means grams of solute in 100 mL of solution.
Formula: (grams of solute ÷ millilitres of solution) × 100.
slides.notes: Write the formula on the board and work through one example: 5 g of salt in 100 mL of solution gives (5 ÷ 100) × 100 = 5%. Then ask: 'If we double the salt to 10 g in the same 100 mL of solution, what is the percent?' [10%.] If a learner answers 5% again, they may be confused about what doubles; remind them the mass changed but the volume stayed the same. Tell learners they will use this formula in the activity, so write it in their notebooks now. Timing: about 3 minutes. No safety reminder needed.

slides.title: Reading a graduated cylinder
lines: Place the cylinder on a flat table.
Bend down so your eyes are level with the liquid surface.
Read the mark at the bottom of the curved surface.
slides.notes: Demonstrate with a real graduated cylinder if you have one. Place it on a flat table, pour water, and show how the water surface curves up at the edges. Explain that we read the bottom of the curve, called the meniscus. Ask two volunteers to read the volume at eye level and tell the class their reading. Safety reminder: glass cylinders can break, so carry them with two hands, never use a cracked cylinder, and wipe up spills immediately so no one slips. Timing: about 3 minutes. Tell learners they will do this in their groups next.

slides.title: Make and measure two solutions
lines: 1. Put 5 g of salt in the cup.
2. Add about 60 mL of water. Stir to dissolve.
3. Pour into the cylinder. Top up to 100 mL.
4. Label: 5 g per 100 mL of solution.
5. Repeat with 10 g of sugar.

image.alt: A spoon pouring granular solid (likely sugar or salt) into a glass of water, with particles shown falling and some dissolved at the bottom.

slides.notes: Organize groups of 4-6 and assign roles: measurer, weigher, stirrer, recorder. Read the steps aloud and show how to place the cylinder on a flat table and read at eye level. Walk around and check that groups read the volume correctly and record both mass and volume. Ask: 'Which solution is more concentrated, the salt or the sugar one?' [The sugar one: 10% compared with 5%.] Safety: do not taste any solution; wash hands with soap and water after handling; handle glass carefully and clean spills at once. Follow school rules for disposing of the used solutions. Timing: about 15 minutes. Additional note for the teacher: Emphasize that percent mass/volume refers to the final solution volume, so learners must dissolve the solute first and then top up to the final volume, not measure the water first and then add solute.

slides.title: What is the concentration?
lines: 8 g of sugar is dissolved in water to make 200 mL of solution. What is the concentration?
slides.notes: Read the question and all four choices. Give learners 60 seconds of quiet thinking time. Ask them to show their answer by holding up one finger for 2%, two fingers for 4%, three for 8%, four for 16%. Do not reveal the answer. Watch for common errors: 2% usually means the learner halved 4% or used 400 mL; 8% means they divided by 100 instead of 200; 16% means they doubled instead of dividing. Note how many chose each option so you can address it in the reveal. Timing: about 2 minutes. No safety reminder needed.

slides.title: Answer: 4%
lines: 0.04 × 100 = 4% mass/volume
slides.notes: Reveal the correct answer and work through the calculation step by step on the board. Explain that we divide the mass of the solute by the volume of the solution, then multiply by 100 to make it a percent. Ask: 'Why do we divide by 200 mL and not by 100?' [Because the solution was made up to 200 mL, and concentration describes the whole solution.] If many learners chose 8%, point out that dividing by 100 gives a different number and is only correct when the volume is exactly 100 mL. Ask one learner to repeat the formula in their own words. Timing: about 3 minutes.

slides.title: Remember today
lines: Concentration tells how much solute is in a certain amount of solution.
Percent mass/volume = (grams of solute ÷ millilitres of solution) × 100.
Read a graduated cylinder on a flat table, at eye level, at the bottom of the curve.
slides.notes: Read the summary aloud and give learners one minute to copy it. Tell them these three points are what they should remember for the exit ticket and for the rest of the week. Then give the exit ticket on paper: 'If you dissolve 8 g of sugar in water to make 200 mL of solution, what is the concentration in percent mass/volume?' The expected answer is 4%: 8 ÷ 200 = 0.04, then 0.04 × 100 = 4%. Remind learners to wash hands after handling the salt and sugar and to return the glassware carefully. Collect the papers as learners finish. Timing: about 5 minutes.

slides.title: Day 3: Heat and Dissolving
lines: Today: We will find out if warm water dissolves salt faster than cold water.
slides.notes: Welcome the class and point to the title. Say: today we continue our solutions topic. We will compare cold and warm water. Ask: 'Who has stirred Milo or juice in water at home?' Let two or three learners share briefly. Remind them that yesterday they measured concentration in grams per 100 mL. Tell them today they will use a fair test: change only the water temperature, keep the amount of salt, the water, and the stirring the same. Keep this to about one minute, then move on.

slides.title: Which dissolves faster?
lines: What do you think: will salt dissolve faster in cold water or in warm water?
slides.notes: Pose this question before any explanation. Let learners predict by a show of hands: cold or warm. Do not confirm the answer yet. Ask one learner to explain their thinking. Accept answers such as 'warm because it's hot' or 'cold because juice stays cold'. Say: 'We will test this today and find out for sure.' Record a few predictions on the board so the class can compare at the end. This sets up the investigation and builds curiosity.

slides.title: Warm water dissolves many solids faster
lines: In warm water, many solid solutes dissolve faster than in cold water.
In our test, salt should disappear sooner in warm water.
slides.notes: Explain in plain language: warm water particles move faster. They bump into the salt or sugar pieces more often, so the pieces break apart and spread into the water more quickly. Point to the drawing: the warm cup shows faster dissolving. Ask: 'Based on this, what do we expect in our test?' Expected: warm water dissolves the salt faster. Tell learners they will soon see this for themselves. Keep the statement honest: many solid solutes dissolve faster in warm water, but not every substance behaves the same way. Add: 'The warm water is warm, not boiling.'

slides.title: Solubility and stirring
lines: solubility — the most solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature.
stirring — makes dissolving faster but does not change how much can dissolve.
slides.notes: Write the two meanings on the board. Say: solubility is like a limit for how much salt can dissolve in a cup of water at a certain temperature. Stirring helps the salt disappear faster, but it cannot make the cup hold more salt than the limit. Ask: 'If I stir and stir, can I dissolve more salt than without stirring?' Expected: no, stirring only makes it faster. Correct the wrong answer: some learners think stirring increases the amount; explain that the limit depends on the solute, solvent, and temperature, not on stirring. Have learners copy the two terms.

slides.title: Salt in cold and warm water
lines: 1. Label two cups C (cold) and W (warm).
2. Add one teaspoon of salt to each cup at the same time.
3. Watch without stirring. Record how long the salt takes to disappear.
4. Stir both cups and record again.
Note: Do not taste or drink. Use warm, not boiling, water.
slides.notes: Before starting: safety reminder. Do not taste or drink the salt water. Use only warm water, not boiling. The teacher checks the water temperature first. Wipe spills at once. Organise groups of four to six. Give each group two cups, a graduated cylinder or marked cup, salt, a teaspoon, water, and a stirrer. Have learners measure 100 mL of water into each cup. One learner adds salt to both cups at the same time; another stirs both cups at the same rate. Continue adding salt and stirring until solid remains. Record the total teaspoons that dissolved. Circulate and ask: 'Which cup dissolved more salt? Which cup dissolved faster?' Expected: the warm cup dissolved more and faster. Remind groups not to pour out water until told.

slides.title: Which water dissolves sugar faster?
lines: In which water will a teaspoon of sugar dissolve faster?
choices: Neither, because sugar does not dissolve
slides.notes: Read the question aloud and give 30 seconds of thinking time. Ask learners to answer with hand signs: one finger for cold, two for warm, three for both the same, four for neither. Do not reveal yet. Note who chooses cold water or 'both the same'. This is a quick check of whether learners link heat with faster dissolving and greater solubility. Keep the pace brisk. Say: 'Hold your answer. Let's see.' Then go to the reveal slide. The answer is not on this slide.

slides.title: Warm water dissolves sugar faster
lines: Warm water dissolves sugar faster and can dissolve more sugar overall.
Warm water particles move faster, so they hit sugar particles more often.
Warm water also has a higher solubility limit for sugar.
slides.notes: Reveal the answer: warm water. Explain that warm water particles move faster and bump into the sugar particles more often, pulling them into the solution more quickly. Warm water can also dissolve a greater maximum amount of sugar. Ask: 'Does stirring change how much sugar can dissolve, or only how fast?' Expected: only how fast. If a learner chose cold water, respond: cold water slows dissolving; it does not speed it up. If a learner chose 'both the same', remind them of today's observation with salt. Link back to the predictions on the board.

slides.title: Our big idea today
lines: Warm water makes many solid solutes dissolve faster.
Warm water can often dissolve a greater maximum amount of solute than cold water.
Stirring makes dissolving faster but does not change how much can dissolve.
There is a limit to how much solute can dissolve at a given temperature.
slides.notes: Have learners copy these lines. Ask one or two learners to say the big idea in their own words: heat makes many solid solutes dissolve faster and can dissolve more. Remind them that stirring only changes the speed, not the amount. Mention that there is a limit called solubility. Tell them tomorrow they will test solutions with litmus paper to see if they are acids, bases, or salts. Collect the exit-ticket papers before the bell. This is the last slide of the day.

slides.title: Day 4: Testing with Litmus
lines: Today: We will test common solutions and group them as acids, bases, or salts.
slides.notes: Open the lesson with a calm, clear voice. Hold up one red litmus strip and one blue litmus strip so learners can see the paper. Say: 'Today we will use these small papers to test liquids safely.' Do not reveal results. Ask learners to look at the intro line and predict how many categories we will use. Expected answers: three categories (acid, base, salt), or maybe two. Accept all ideas. This is the hook; no answer should be given yet. Remind learners that all tasting is forbidden. Time: about 2 minutes.

slides.title: What Do You Think?
lines: Think about calamansi juice you have tasted in food at home.
What flavour was it?
slides.notes: Ask this as a whole-class question. Expected answer: sour. Accept other answers like 'sweet' or 'bitter' but steer toward sour. Ask: 'What do you think makes sour foods sour?' Let two or three learners answer. Do not correct ideas yet. Say: 'In science, we do not rely on taste alone, because not all liquids are safe. We use a test paper.'
