This sets up the purpose of litmus. Time: about 2 minutes. Keep responses short; praise all ideas to encourage participation. Note: Do not ask learners to taste anything in class; the question refers to past experiences with food.

slides.title: Litmus Paper
lines: Litmus is a special paper made from a natural dye.
It changes color when it touches an acid or a base.
Red and blue litmus papers give different color changes.

image.alt: Several thin litmus paper strips, one being dipped into a shallow dish of liquid.

slides.notes: Explain that litmus is not a food and must never be put in the mouth. It is an indicator, meaning it shows a change in color. Show the drawing and point to the strips. Say: 'We will use red and blue litmus, because each one tells us something different.' Do not give the two rules yet; that comes next. Ask: 'Why do we need a test paper instead of tasting?' Expected answers: because some liquids are dangerous, because taste can be fooled, because it is safer. Time: about 2 minutes. Keep the strips dry except when dipping.

slides.title: How Litmus Reacts
lines: Acids turn blue litmus red.
Bases turn red litmus blue.
Table salt (sodium chloride) solution is neutral: it does not change red or blue litmus.
slides.notes: Read the two rules aloud with the class. Use choral reading once. Then ask two learners to restate them. Check understanding by asking: 'If blue litmus turns red, is the liquid an acid or a base?' Expected answer: acid. Repeat for red litmus turning blue: base. Add the neutral idea: 'Some solutions, like table salt solution, do not change either paper. We call them neutral.' Do not say all salt solutions are always neutral; for this lesson, table salt solution is neutral, but remind learners that litmus tells us acid or base only. Some salts, like baking soda, actually give a basic solution. Time: about 3 minutes.

slides.title: Our Four Test Solutions
lines: 1. Vinegar
2. Calamansi juice
3. Baking soda solution
4. Table salt solution
slides.notes: Hold up each labelled cup and name it. Ask: 'Which of these might you find at home?' (all). Explain that baking soda solution is made by mixing baking soda in water; the teacher prepares it. Remind learners: these are for testing only, not for drinking. Safety: the teacher pours small amounts into cups; learners do not pour from large bottles. If any learner has an allergy or sensitive skin, seat them away from splashes and allow them to observe with the group recorder. Time: about 3 minutes. Do not reveal which is acid, base, or salt yet.

slides.title: Safety First
lines: Do not taste or drink any test solution.
Wash your hands with soap and water after testing.
Use a new strip for each test and place used paper in the waste cup.
slides.notes: Read each rule and have learners repeat the first rule after you. Explain that even vinegar and calamansi juice, which are weak acids, can sting the eyes or a cut. So keep fingers away from eyes and mouth during the activity. Show the handwashing picture and point out the soap and water. Tell learners where the waste cup is. Safety reminder: no eating or drinking during the activity; learners with open cuts on their hands should cover them or ask the teacher for help. Time: about 2 minutes. Model handwashing before dismissal.

slides.title: Activity: Test Each Solution
lines: 1. Dip a red strip for 5 seconds.
2. Record its colour.
3. Repeat with a blue strip.
4. Test all four solutions.
slides.notes: Demonstrate steps 1 and 2 with vinegar in front of the class. Explain that they must dip only the tip and not stir hard, so the paper does not tear. Tell learners to use one strip for red litmus and a new strip for blue litmus in each solution, and never to reuse a strip. Group roles: materials manager, tester, recorder, reporter. Large class tip: set a timer for 8 minutes and announce the halfway mark. Safety: keep the cups in the middle of the table, not near the edge; if a cup spills, raise a hand and do not wipe with bare hands. Time: about 10 minutes. Walk around to check proper use of equipment. Remind learners to record the solution name, red litmus color, blue litmus color, and classification on their printed record sheet.

slides.title: What Results Should We Compare?
lines: Vinegar and calamansi juice turned blue litmus red: they are acids.
Baking soda solution turned red litmus blue: it is a base.
Table salt solution did not change either litmus: it is neutral.
slides.notes: This is the class summary. Ask reporters to share one result each; write them on the board table. If groups disagree, ask them to look at the strip again, but strips may dry and change slightly, so use recorded colors. Common wrong idea: 'If it does not change, it is not a solution.' Respond: 'Table salt solution is still a solution; it just does not change litmus because it is neutral.' Another wrong idea: 'All acids are dangerous.' Respond: 'Vinegar and calamansi juice are weak acids we use in food, but we still do not taste them in the lab.' Time: about 4 minutes. Praise careful observation.

slides.title: Red litmus in vinegar
lines: Red litmus paper is dipped into vinegar. What happens?
slides.notes: This is the exit ticket. Read the question once and tell learners to answer on paper, individually. Do not let them call out. Remind them: red litmus and blue litmus behave differently. If a learner chooses 'It turns blue', they may be mixing up which paper changes with an acid; note this and reteach during the reveal. Give 3 minutes. Collect papers or have learners hold them up. Keep materials off the table during the exit ticket so attention is on the question. Safety: after the exit ticket, collect all test strips and solutions.

slides.title: Answer
lines: It stays red.
Vinegar is an acid, and acids turn blue litmus red, not red litmus blue.
slides.notes: Reveal the correct answer. Say: 'Vinegar is an acid. Acids change blue litmus to red. So red litmus stays red, because it only changes when the liquid is a base.' Ask learners who chose 'It turns blue' to explain their thinking, then correct gently. Check that learners can say the rule in their own words. Remind the class to wash hands with soap and water and to place used paper in the waste cup. Congratulate them for safe and careful work. Time: about 3 minutes. Collect materials and dismiss learners by table group.

slides.title: Day 5: Review and Assess
lines: Today: We review solutions and plan a safe investigation.
slides.notes: Welcome the class and set a calm tone for assessment day. Say: 'This week we learned about solutions — solute, solvent, concentration, solubility, and litmus. Today we review and you show what you know.' Ask: 'What are the two parts of a solution?' Expect 'solute and solvent.' If a learner says 'water' only, respond: 'Water is often the solvent, but a solution always has both a solute and a solvent.' Keep this to one minute, then move on. Remind learners that the written assessment is individual and quiet.

slides.title: What are the parts of a solution?
lines: Think of salt water. What dissolves, and what does the dissolving?

image.alt: A glass of water with tiny particles spreading evenly throughout the liquid to show a solution.

slides.notes: Give learners 20 seconds to think, then take 3–4 answers. Expected: salt is the solute (it dissolves) and water is the solvent (it does the dissolving). A common wrong answer is 'the salt disappears' — respond: 'The salt is still there; its particles are spread evenly in the water.' Do not reveal more than this; the full summary comes later. Keep the pace quick so you have time for the assessment.

slides.title: What we will do today
lines: 1. Show what you know in a short written assessment.
2. Plan a safe investigation with your group.
3. Share one safety rule with the class.
slides.notes: Read the three outcomes aloud slowly. Explain that the assessment is individual and quiet, and that the planning task is group work. Tell learners how long each part will take so they can manage their time. Ask: 'What does it mean to work quietly on your own?' Expect answers like 'no talking' and 'no copying.' For large classes, remind row leaders how they will collect papers. This slide is only two minutes.

slides.title: Written assessment
lines: 1. Write your name on your answer sheet.
2. Read each item carefully before answering.
3. You have 18 minutes to complete all 7 items.
4. Pass your paper to the row leader when time is up.
slides.notes: Distribute papers face down, then tell learners to turn them over together. Set a visible timer for 18 minutes. Walk around but do not give answers. If a learner asks for help, say: 'Do your best; we will review later.' Watch for learners looking at a seatmate's paper and quietly move them apart if needed. At the end, have row leaders collect papers. Do not discuss answers yet.

slides.title: Plan: how much salt is in salt water?
lines: 1. List your materials.
2. Write safe steps: evaporate the water, then weigh the salt.
3. Show how to calculate concentration: (g of solute ÷ mL of solution) × 100.

image.alt: A measuring cup and a graduated cylinder with liquid inside.

slides.notes: Explain the task in plain words: 'You have a sample of salt water. You want to find out how much salt is dissolved in it.' Ask: 'If we evaporate the water, what is left?' Expect 'the salt.' Ask: 'How do we get percent mass per volume?' Expect 'divide the mass of salt by the volume of solution, then multiply by 100.' Safety: no tasting; handle glass carefully; learners use sun/warm-place evaporation only; if the teacher demonstrates heating, learners wear goggles and stay an arm's length away, the dish is moved only with tongs onto a heat-proof mat, and heating stops while a little liquid remains to avoid spitting hot salt; wash hands after. Give groups 8 minutes and walk around to check their safety steps.

slides.title: Which step is safe and accurate?
lines: Choose the best way to read the volume of a liquid in a graduated cylinder.
choices: Hold the cylinder in your hand and read from above.
Place it on a flat surface and read at eye level.
Read it while it is tilted.
Read from below the liquid surface.
slides.notes: Give learners 30 seconds to think, then take answers from 2-3 groups before revealing. Common wrong answer: reading from above or holding the cylinder. Respond: 'Tilting or reading at an angle changes the volume you see.' The reveal is on the next slide. This check takes about one minute; do not spend longer, because the exit ticket still follows.

slides.title: Answer: Flat surface and eye level
lines: Place it on a flat surface and read at eye level.
This gives an accurate volume and prevents tipping.
slides.notes: Reveal the answer and explain: 'A flat surface keeps the cylinder from tipping, and reading at eye level avoids parallax error - that means the volume looks different if you read from above or below.' Ask one learner to say why holding it in the air is not safe. Then tell groups to check that their written plan uses this rule. This should take about one minute; move on to the summary.

slides.title: Remember these key ideas
lines: A solution has a solute dissolved in a solvent.
Concentration can be written as grams of solute per 100 mL of solution.
Heat and stirring speed up dissolving; heat also often increases solubility.
Litmus: acids turn blue litmus red; bases turn red litmus blue.
No change means neutral, not 'a salt'.
slides.notes: Read each line aloud and ask learners to copy them into their notebooks. Check understanding by asking one quick question per line, for example: 'In salt water, which is the solute?' (salt). 'What does litmus paper tell us?' (whether a solution is an acid or a base). These lines match what the written assessment covered, so copying them is good review. Keep this to five minutes.

slides.title: What is one safe way to use a graduated cylinder?
lines: Choose the best answer.
choices: Place it on a flat surface and read at eye level.
Hold it high in the air while reading.
slides.notes: Read the question aloud and have learners answer on small slips of paper or by raising hands. Give 30 seconds. Do not hint at the answer. Common wrong answer: filling it with boiling water — respond later that boiling water can burn and should be handled only by the teacher. Collect answers, then reveal on the next slide. This is a practice check, not the exit ticket.

slides.title: Answer: Flat surface and eye level
lines: Place it on a flat surface and read at eye level.
This gives an accurate volume and prevents tipping.
slides.notes: Reveal the answer and explain: 'A flat surface keeps the cylinder from tipping, and reading at eye level avoids parallax error — that means the volume looks different if you read from above or below.' Ask one learner to name another safety rule from the week. Then give the exit ticket on paper: 'You dissolve 6 g of salt in water to make 150 mL of solution. What is the concentration in % mass/volume? Show your work.' The answer is 4% because 6 ÷ 150 = 0.04, and 0.04 × 100 = 4%. Collect the slips as learners leave.
